description:
FILED s473p (Opus, 2026-09-07) while shipping #1200's transpile half.

WHAT IS LEFT.  #1200 put a string eval's EMISSION on disk, so the pl2cl round
trip (~16 ms of an eval's ~21 ms) is paid once ever.  The other ~5 ms is SBCL
reading and evaluating that text, EVERY RUN, and it is removable the same way
modules' is (#1188): compile the cached .lisp once, load the fasl thereafter.
MEASURED on the PCL core, one eval-shaped CL text (scratch/s473p/probe1.lisp,
s473p's worktree):
    READ + EVAL of the text     5.00 ms
    COMPILE-FILE of the text   10.00 ms   (paid ONCE)
    LOADING the fasl            0.05 ms
So an all-hit `use JSON::PP; print 1` (80 evals) would lose a further ~0.4 s
off the 0.409 s #1200 leaves — the biggest single number remaining in the
yardstick's constants (plan-speed-and-ir-s470 §A.4.1).

THE BLOCKER, and it is not the cache: **`load` cannot hand back the value of a
file's LAST FORM**, and p-eval's value IS that form's value (its READ+EVAL loop
returns the last one).  Three shapes were considered and each is written down
so they are not re-derived:

 (a) WRAP the last form as `(setf *p-eval-fasl-value* <form>)`.  This destroys
     the form's TOP-LEVEL-ness, and with it every `:compile-toplevel` effect
     its macros have — for `p-sub` that is `%p-reserve-sub-name`, the
     shadow+intern the READER depends on (#1188's own commentary).  A CL
     `(setf v (eval-when (:load-toplevel :execute) …))` still RUNS the body at
     load (CLHS: a non-toplevel eval-when with :execute is an implicit progn),
     so it looks fine on the common shapes and silently loses the compile-time
     half.  Not safe without a classifier, and a classifier over "which macros
     need top-level processing" is the thing rule 11 says not to build.
 (b) SPLIT: compile every form BUT the last into the fasl, read+eval the last
     from the cached text.  Correct by construction and worth NOTHING — the
     prefix of an eval's emission is `(p-defpackage …) (in-package …)
     (p-declare-sub …) (defvar …)`, all cheap, and the expensive form IS the
     last one (the `p-sub`, or the body expression).
 (c) Have the EMITTER mark the value form (a `--server` response field, or a
     wrapper the transpiler emits because it knows which statement is last).
     This is the only shape that keeps both properties, and it is a compiler
     change, not a runtime one — which is why it is a task and not a filler.

WHAT ELSE IT NEEDS: the compile must run with *pcl-fasl-build* bound, exactly
as a module's does (an eval body has the same BEGIN / sub-install ordering
question), and the fasl must be keyed by *pcl-runtime-identity* on top of
#1200's key, since a fasl carries this runtime's macro expansions.

AND A COST TO SIZE FIRST: a never-repeated eval would pay a COMPILE-FILE
(10 ms) on top of the transpile it already pays.  Measured population: three
eval-heavy perl-tests files run 842 evals of which 652 are distinct.  So the
build must be deferred — the cheapest shape is "build the fasl on the first
.lisp HIT", i.e. never on the run that first meets the text — or gated on a
size/count rule.  #1200 deliberately writes only the text for this reason.

BAR when taken: #1200's own (gate, full sweep, the eval-cache guard file, the
cold-vs-warm population run) plus the five semantic probes #1200 lists, since
a fasl RUNS the forms rather than handing back text.
subject: The other half of #1200: a cached string eval should load a FASL, not re-compile its text -- blocked on getting the last form's VALUE out of a load
